background_notes.fact: If f:A→B is a bijective isometry between Euclidean subsets, then for every s>0 and δ>0 their ambient Hausdorff contents H^s_δ agree, hence H^s(A)=H^s(B).

The Euclidean product distance makes this coordinate map an isometry.

background_notes.justification: Intersect any cover of A with A and map the intersections by f to obtain a countable cover of B with no greater diameters; empty intersections cause no cost. Apply the inverse isometry to intersected covers of B for the reverse inequality. Infima and then suprema over the same positive scales give equality.

background_notes.fact: For 0<ρ≤1, N=ceil(1/ρ) is a positive finite integer with 1/N≤ρ and N≤2/ρ. The N closed intervals [j/N,(j+1)/N], 0≤j<N, cover [0,1]. If diam(U)≤ρ in ℝ^n and J is one such interval, then diam(U×J)≤√2ρ in the specified Euclidean metric.

grounds.reason: Squared product distance is the sum of squared coordinate distances.

background_notes.justification: The integer ceiling obeys x≤ceil(x)≤x+1; apply x=1/ρ≥1 and invert positive quantities for 1/N≤ρ. The adjacent subdivision intervals cover [0,1] and have diameter 1/N. For any two product points each coordinate distance is≤ρ, so their squared Euclidean distance is≤2ρ². Taking nonnegative square roots and then the diameter supremum proves the bound.

background_notes.fact: For K⊆ℕ and positive finite integers N_i, the set of pairs (i,j) with i∈K and 0≤j<N_i is at most countable. For nonnegative costs c_ij, its total cost equals ∑_{i∈K}∑_{j<N_i}c_ij. Termwise inequalities and multiplication by finite nonnegative constants preserve these sums.

grounds.reason: K⊆ℕ and the covering family are supplied by F002.
Each N_i is a positive finite integer and each product cost is nonnegative; ∑r_i^q<ε.

background_notes.justification: The pair index set injects into ℕ×ℕ, which admits a diagonal enumeration. A nonnegative countable sum is the supremum of its finite subsums. Every finite pair set meets finitely many rows, and finite row subsums are themselves finite pair subsums; these two comparisons give the grouping equality. The same definition gives termwise monotonicity and finite scalar multiplication, including when an intermediate sum is infinite.

background_notes.fact: For s>0, real powers on nonnegative finite bases are increasing, with 0^s=0. On positive bases they satisfy (ab)^s=a^s b^s and ρ^(q+1)/ρ=ρ^q. Consequently, for q>0, 0<ρ≤1, N≤2/ρ, and d_j≤√2ρ, one has ∑_{j<N}d_j^(q+1)≤2(√2)^(q+1)ρ^q.

background_notes.justification: For positive bases, a^s=exp(s log a); monotonicity of log and exp and their addition identities give the asserted power laws and monotonicity. The zero base follows from the positive-exponent convention. Bound each of the N costs by (√2ρ)^(q+1), multiply by N≤2/ρ, and use the positive-base identities to obtain the displayed estimate. The constant 2(√2)^(q+1) is finite and positive for finite real q.

background_notes.fact: For a finite C>0 and x∈[0,∞], if x<Cε for every ε>0 then x=0. A supremum of zero scale contents is zero. For finite real D and b∈[0,∞], if b≤q+1 for every real q>D then b≤D+1; likewise b≤a for all a>1 implies b≤1.

background_notes.justification: Choosing ε=1 first rules out x=∞. If finite x>0, choosing ε=x/(2C)>0 contradicts x<Cε; hence x=0. Supremum of a family all equal to zero is zero. Choosing q=D+1 first makes b finite; if b>D+1, choose q=D+(b-D-1)/2, so q>D and q+1<b, a contradiction. For the last assertion a=2 first makes b finite, and if b>1 choose a=(1+b)/2. These are order arguments and involve no interchange of limits with sums or infima.
